Skype Music

By: Diana Lucas | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Students from Soweto inspired and taught by renowned musicians from United Kingdom

Summary:
Njabulo ,a music student from South Africa, who has talent but no means to reach for the sky and develop her gift.
A musician from United Kingdom’s Birmingham Conservatoire. Two totally different worlds, which now have the opportunity to interact.

This is Arco a collaborative music project between Soweto’s Morris Isaacson School and Birmingham Conservatoire Strings department. Twenty four gifted students from Soweto were selected at the beginning of this year to participate in weekly instrumental Skype lessons given by teachers at Birmingham Conservatoire – this is in addition to their music lessons in South Africa.

Their aim: to provide life-changing inspiration of music to children who would never normally have access in their belief that music is a tool transcending both language and cultural boundaries. To provide support and opportunity to students at who may not readily have access and exposure to such a rich international cultural exchange of this caliber.

These 24 students are only coached and mentored by students and alumni of the Conservatoire but have access to live event streaming of master classes, workshops and performances taking place in the Strings Department at the Conservatoire and have been inspired, exposed and participated in music and performance at a top international level.

The teachers in Birmingham on their apart have gained valuable experience in teaching, chamber music coaching, technical videoing skills and a cultural awareness outside their normal life. It is a two way street.


Further information:
Birmingham Conservatoire Head of Strings Louise Lansdown who is from South Africa is over the moon at the success of this project “Arco is a project of sharing, learning, building and inspiring and one that will be a privilege to be a part of. The impossible is now possible due to the incredible development of technology and we are able forge worlds together around the common denominator of music.
In August the teachers from Birmingham will be in South Africa, to meet the students they have been video conferencing and live streaming, we will profile students and teachers, what have they each got out of this collaborative project. How their Skype music educational journey impacted on the lives both sides of the video.
Is this the way forward to educate the next generation of musicians? A beginning of a long term partnership that will not just bring the world’s experts to Soweto but Soweto’s musicians to the world.


Expert:
Dr. Louise Lansdown

Press Release:


Birmingham Conservatoire
How has access to the internet enabled students from Soweto to be inspired and taught by musicians from the United Kingdom’s prestigious Birmingham Conservatoire? Carte Blanche witnesses the harmonious collision of classical music and cutting edge technology.


Script:


V/O 12 sec

Aspiring, music students from Soweto

Musicians, from United Kingdom’s Birmingham Conservatoire.

Two totally different world’s, come together.

It all started about a year ago….

Louise: I have had numerous dangerous ideas in my lifetime and once I have the idea that’s it its going to happen hell or high water……

V/O 9 sec
Violinist, Louise Lansdown left South Africa …as part of the mass exodus of top class classical musicians in the late 90’s.

Louise: Many of SA orchestras closed and music departments had huge problems. I was amongst so many of my generation who felt that if we wanted to aspire to greatest possible heights would need to go somewhere else…

V/O 14 sec
Flash forward 17 years and Louise now Head of Strings at the renowned Birmingham Conservatoire, started looking for a way to give back to the country she had gained so much from in the way of music.

LINK
Louise was faced with a challenge how could she take the opportunities and facilities of Birmingham and transport them to Soweto

Louise: Sitting in the usual light deprived coffee shop in B looking at the grey miserable weather outside and somehow a light bulb just flashed in my head and SKYPe just shone at me and live streaming and that was the idea.

V/O 15 sec
Her students, her musicians without leaving Birmingham would teach schoolchildren showing promise in Soweto. The Cape Gate Miagi Centre for Music situated in the heart of the township bought in to Louis’s brainwave

LINK
It took some time for Louise to get the ARCO project together but at the beginning of the year 24 gifted students were finally accepted

V/O 4 sec
And 16 year old violin student Sinethemba’ was one of them.

Sinethemba: This whole Skype project has really encouraged me more to listen to classical music
Derek: And who are your heroes in the classical world?
Pteter Tchaivosky I don’t know how to say his name, very tricky but I really like him.
Derek We use Skype for interviews sometimes difficulties, here?
Sinethemba: Sometimes no connection and one time we tried to fix connection for about 25 minutes and my lesson is only 30 minutes so we didn’t get to do anything.

V/O 3 sec
Martha Evans is Sinethemba’s Skype teacher….

Derek: What do you think of this connection between Birmingham and Soweto?
Martha: It is so inspiring I think it’s really two fold so there is a real opportunity for us a students to hone our teaching skills and the opportunity we are giving to the kids here is really positive as well both sides a real sense we are achieving something.

V/O 5 sec
Tiny -Sinethemba’s mother doesn’t recognise this new daughter of hers

Tiny: No she enjoys it so much at times like yesterday she was in the kitchen and then after some time you find her in her bedroom practising.

V/O 10 sec
Every week 14 Birmingham strings students and a few of the teachers including Louise mentor and teach the Soweto students, no one is paid.

Louise :I have the grave yard slot 7 am UK time 6 am in UK summer I thought it was too cruel to ask any of my students to teach that early …
Derek: And you do it with a smile?
Louise: I often wear my pyjama when I am they are always smiling at me and ….I am freezing in my pyjama’s and dressing gown with my viola stuck to my chin.

V/O 7 sec
Violin teacher at Miagi, Olga Maraba has seen her pupils grow in the six months of their Skype lessons.

Olga: When I started playing violin I never had this opportunity the kids are very inspired and excited and afterwards we are just going to have good results I am hoping.

V/O 4 sec
15 year old Njabulo’s football friends are amazed at his new passion.

Njabulo: They think I am the only boy playing violin in Soweto I just love the sound when I hear someone play the violin I cry.

Link: This is a very special week for the Soweto students it’s the first time they are meeting their virtual teachers without an internet connection

V/O 4 sec
And the sound of music fills every corner of the centre.

Derek : What like meeting Martha for the first time face to face?
Sinethemba: It was amazing Who usually see her on the screen and now she is here.

Martha: Its really challenging teaching through the screen we can touch each other tension in the left hand is really hard to sense over the screen and hard to teach so the hands on approach over the last 5 days is really important,

V/O 7 sec
For 15 year old Lindo who had never played the Viola before this year, meeting Eileen was indescribable.

Lindo : It kinda of felt like a dream, now talking to live we have been discussing pieces I play and slide from finger point…I tell her about my school and how things are doing.

Derek: Alistair this must be so much easier than Skype?
Alistair: So much easier specially with string playing so much to do with tension.
Derek: Have you been able to discuss football at all?
Alistair: I’ve introduced him to my favourite team and hopefully he is going to wear his Liverpool top with pride

V/O 9 sec
The Skype teachers used creative ways of fundraising to pay there way out here.. Alistair symbolically ran the length of South Africa’s coast line.

Alistair: 2 700 km ..I achieved it before I came.
Derek: And collected some money along the way.
Alistair: Yes

V/O 6 sec
The five days culminated in a concert, with everyone playing their part…Soweto and Birmingham in perfect harmony

LINK
So could this be a start of project that not only brings the worlds experts to Soweto but takes Soweto musicians to the world

Louise We are going to bring some teachers from here to us in Birmingham and we want to send our students come and live here and teach here and we want Arco students to come and study it is really bringing 2 cities together\
Louise: Not going to give up not a giver upper
Derek: You’re very determined
Louise: Very
